findings.citation_text: Wireless signals have also been exploited by researchers for sound recovery [8]–[13]. Hu et al. [11] introduced mmEcho, which uses mmWave to measure vibrations for eavesdropping, while Hu et al. [10] developed MILLIEAR, which reconstructs audio from vibrations using generative models. Wei et al. [9] demonstrated acoustic eavesdropping using WiFi signals, and Wang et al. [12] expanded eavesdropping through Impulse Radio Ultra-Wideband (IR-UWB) technology with their UWHear system. RFID-based methods have also been explored, with Wang et al. [13] showing how audio can be intercepted via RFID.
